newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt studies soldier's Bloody Sunday claim.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt studies soldier's Bloody Sunday claim.

text.p: A British soldier said in remarks published on Sunday that his platoon was given "shoot to kill" orders on the eve of "Bloody Sunday," when 13 unarmed Northern Ireland demonstrators were killed by army gunfire.

The unnamed soldier told the Sunday Business Post in direct contradiction of official accounts of the 1972 shooting that none of the demonstrators he saw was armed and some of his colleagues continued to shoot at them after a ceasefire order.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said the government was studying the soldier's statement before deciding whether to present it to Britain as part of Dublin's efforts to secure a new investigation into the shooting.
"Any new evidence has to be examined very thoroughly and this is what we are doing at the moment," Spring told reporters.
The Buisness Post report was believed to be the first published recollection by one of the British soldiers who opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in Londonderry on January 30, 1972.

His statement directly contradicted the official army and British government version of the day's events and was seen as further ammunition for relatives of the dead who want an official British apology for the killings.

An official 1972 investigation by the Chief Justice, Lord Widgery, exonerated the paratroopers of blame accepting that they believed they were under fire from Irish Republican Army (IRA) gunmen fighting British rule.

The soldier said a British official tore up the evidence he had planned to give to the Widgery tribunal and he was given another statement "which bore no relation to the facts" to provide to the investigation.

The demonstration, in support of civil rights grievances by Northern Ireland's 40 percent Catholic minority, was a turning point in Northern Ireland's troubled history and a recruiting coup for the Catholic-backed IRA.

Soldier A, as the newspaper called him, told the Business Post that troops sent to Londondery to quell civil rights demonstrations by Catholic Irish nationalists were told to shoot to kill and ignored orders to stop shooting.
He quoted an officer as telling his platoon: "Let's teach these buggers a lesson - we want some kills tomorrow."
Soldier A said he saw evidence of "strikes" - a British army expression for shots fired at troops - when his platoon was ordered in to quell one part of the demonstration.

"I raised my rifle and aimed, but on tracking across the people in front of me, could see women and children although the majority were men, all widly shouting but could see no one with a weapon, so I lowered my rifle," he said.

He said that, after an order to cease fire was given, "blokes were getting in while the going was good as people with gleeful expressions were running up from the rear and elbowing their way through to get into the firing line."

The British government says Bloody Sunday was a terrible tragedy but it will not re-open investigations unless it receives fresh evidence, which the Irish government is collating from eyewitnesses and academic studies.

Protestant Unionists, who want the province to stay British, say it was only one incident in a 28-year conflict which killed 3,200 people and blame the IRA for Northern Ireland's descent into guerrilla war.
